claim: ParABS is the most common partitioning system for bacterial chromosomes and low-copy number plasmids.
source: The most common of these, ParABS, consists of ParA, a DNA-binding ATPase and ParB, a protein that binds to centromeric-like parS sequences on the DNA cargo.
evidence: Supported by citations to Badrinarayanan et al., 2015 and Kawalek et al., 2020 in the Introduction section.

claim: ParABS consists of three components: parS (centromeric-like region), ParA (Walker-type ATPase), and ParB protein.
source: The system consists of three components: (i) a centromeric-like region parS, (ii) a Walker-type ATPase ParA, and (iii) the protein ParB.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the system components in the Introduction.

claim: ParA binds DNA non-specifically in its ATP-dependent dimer state and coats the nucleoid.
source: ParA binds DNA non-specifically in its ATP-dependent dimer state and therefore coats the nucleoid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: ParB dimers bind to consensus sequences within parS and spread out several kilobases to form a condensed nucleoprotein complex.
source: ParB dimers bind to, and spread out several kilobases from, consensus sequences within parS to form a condensed nucleoprotein complex, called the partition complex, that is clearly visible using fluorescent microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: ParB stimulates the ATPase activity of ParA, releasing it from the nucleoid and generating a gradient of bound ParA.
source: ParB also stimulates the ATPase activity of ParA releasing it from the nucleoid and generating a gradient of bound ParA around it.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Partition complexes move up the ParA gradient mediated by ParB-ParA bonds connecting the cargo to the nucleoid.
source: Partition complexes are believed to move up this gradient mediated by ParB-ParA bonds connecting the cargo (e.g. a plasmid or chromosomal origin) and the underlying nucleoid.
evidence: This is stated as a current understanding in the Introduction.

claim: Elastic fluctuations of the chromosome and/or ParA-ParB tethers power the directed movement of plasmid cargo according to molecular-scale models.
source: In particular, the most recent molecular-scale models argue that the elastic fluctuations of the chromosome and/or ParA-ParB tethers power the directed movement of the plasmid cargo, while the self-generated ParA gradient specifies the direction (Hu et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2015 and Lim et al., 2014.

claim: ParABS systems fall into three main types (1a, 1b, and chromosomal) based on their phylogeny.
source: ParABS systems fall into three main types based on their phylogeny (Gerdes et al., 2000). Types 1a and 1b are found on plasmids and are distinguished by their genetic organisation and the size of their genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerdes et al., 2000.

claim: Type 1b systems encode much smaller ParA and ParB proteins than type 1a systems and have a broader host range.
source: In particular, type 1b systems encode much smaller ParA and ParB proteins than their type 1a counterparts and have a broader host range, being found in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: ParB from F plasmid and several bacterial species are CTPases.
source: ParB dimers form a DNA clamp that loads onto the DNA at parS sites before sliding (diffusing) along the DNA in a CTP-binding-dependent manner (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019 and Soh et al., 2019.

claim: ParB of type 1b systems do not have the same CTP binding pocket as type 1a systems.
source: Furthermore, the much smaller ParB of the type 1b systems do not have the same CTP binding pocket, yet still confer stability to low-copy plasmids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Cargos are typically located symmetrically at equally-spaced intervals across the nucleoid (regular positioning).
source: Typically, cargos are located symmetrically and at equally-spaced intervals across the the nucleoid i.e. at the mid, quarter or (1/6, 3/6, 5/6) positions for one, two or three cargos respectively (In the case of n cargos, their relative positions are (i-1/2)/n for i = 1, 2, …, n.).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: F plasmid and pB171 have been described as exhibiting oscillatory dynamics.
source: Indeed, both F plasmid and pB171 have been described as exhibiting oscillatory dynamics as they follow corresponding changes in the ParA gradient, which may also lead to regular positioning as a time-averaged effect (Hatano et al., 2007; Ringgaard et al., 2009; Surovtsev et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hatano et al., 2007; Ringgaard et al., 2009; and Surovtsev et al., 2016a.

claim: The lack of quantitative measurements of plasmid dynamics has hindered evaluation of positioning models.
source: While there have been several modelling studies of plasmid positioning (Adachi et al., 2006; Ietswaart et al., 2014; Jindal and Emberly, 2019; Ringgaard et al., 2009; Sugawara and Kaneko, 2011; Walter et al., 2017) and, in particular, two recent stochastic models that incorporate the molecular mechanism of force generation (Hu et al., 2017; Surovtsev et al., 2016a), the lack of quantitative measurements of plasmid dynamics has hindered their evaluation.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field in the Introduction.

claim: F plasmid exhibits true regular positioning as if pulled to its home positions by an over-damped spring-like force.
source: We find unambiguously that the type 1a F plasmid exhibits true regular positioning as if pulled to its home positions by an over-damped spring-like force and we quantitatively reproduce its positioning and segregation behaviour in a unifying stochastic model.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Cells with F plasmid had a median of two ParB foci at birth and four at division under the experimental conditions.
source: Under our conditions, cells had a median of two ParB foci at birth and four at division (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and divided approximately every 100 min.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ParB foci separate within 5 min of plasmid replication.
source: Since ParB foci separate within 5 min of plasmid replication (Onogi et al., 2002; Walter et al., 2020) and there are only a few replication events per cell cycle, in the following we will assume each ParB focus consists of a single plasmid.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Onogi et al., 2002 and Walter et al., 2020.

claim: F plasmid is located at mid-cell in cells with a single plasmid, irrespective of cell length.
source: Consistent with many previous works (Adachi et al., 2006; Hatano et al., 2007; Niki and Hiraga, 1997; Sanchez et al., 2015), we found that F plasmid is, irrespective of length, approximately located at mid-cell in cells with a single plasmid and close to the quarter positions in cells with two plasmids (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C and citations to previous works.

claim: F plasmid is located close to the quarter positions in cells with two plasmids.
source: Consistent with many previous works (Adachi et al., 2006; Hatano et al., 2007; Niki and Hiraga, 1997; Sanchez et al., 2015), we found that F plasmid is, irrespective of length, approximately located at mid-cell in cells with a single plasmid and close to the quarter positions in cells with two plasmids (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D and citations to previous works.

claim: The precision of F plasmid positioning for single plasmids is independent of cell length.
source: We found that the precision of positioning for the single plasmid case was independent of cell length, while for two plasmids it decreased weakly for cell lengths greater than 3 μm, perhaps due to variation in nucleoid segregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For two F plasmids, positioning precision decreases weakly for cell lengths greater than 3 μm.
source: We found that the precision of positioning for the single plasmid case was independent of cell length, while for two plasmids it decreased weakly for cell lengths greater than 3 μm, perhaps due to variation in nucleoid segregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: F plasmid exhibits a clear linear dependence of mean velocity on position along the long cell axis.
source: Analysing cells containing a single plasmid, we found a clear linear dependence of the mean of the velocity on position, while its variance was constant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The variance of F plasmid velocity is constant across positions.
source: Analysing cells containing a single plasmid, we found a clear linear dependence of the mean of the velocity on position, while its variance was constant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The position and velocity autocorrelation functions of F plasmid show no population level evidence of oscillatory behaviour.
source: Furthermore, the position and velocity autocorrelation functions showed no population level evidence of oscillatory behaviour (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The velocity autocorrelation of F plasmid is negative at a lag equal to the sampling time, characteristic of elastic motion.
source: Rather, the velocity autocorrelation was negative at a lag equal to the sampling time, a characteristic of elastic motion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and is a characteristic property of elastic motion.

claim: The observed properties of F plasmid dynamics are characteristic of an over-damped spring-like force.
source: Altogether the observed properties are characteristic of an over-damped spring-like force, similar to that observed for the chromosomal origins of E. coli (Hofmann et al., 2019; Kuwada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and comparison to similar systems.

claim: The characteristic timescale at which elastic fluctuations act on F plasmid is about 2 minutes.
source: Under this model, the slope of the velocity profile is the reciprocal of the characteristic timescale, τ, at which elastic fluctuations act and we found this to be about 2 min.
evidence: This is derived from the velocity profile data in Figure 1E.

claim: The intrinsic diffusion coefficient of F plasmid is (2.27±0.24) x 10^-4 μm²s^-1.
source: We find D=(2.27±0.24) x 10–4 μm2s–1 and keff/(kBT)=36.8 ± 4.1 μm–2 (bounds are the 95% confidence intervals).
evidence: This is derived from fitting the over-damped spring model to experimental data.

claim: The spring constant of the effective force on F plasmid is keff/(kBT)=36.8 ± 4.1 μm^-2.
source: We find D=(2.27±0.24) x 10–4 μm2s–1 and keff/(kBT)=36.8 ± 4.1 μm–2 (bounds are the 95% confidence intervals).
evidence: This is derived from fitting the over-damped spring model to experimental data.

claim: The characteristic force acting on F plasmid is about 0.02 pN.
source: The latter implies a characteristic force of about 0.02 pN acting on the plasmid.
evidence: This is calculated from the spring constant.

claim: At short timescales (1 s), F plasmid dynamics show a linear dependence of MSD on time with a diffusion coefficient of (2.01±0.14) x 10^-4 μm²s^-1.
source: To test this estimate, we tracked plasmid dynamics on a much shorter time-scale (1 s frame rate) at which diffusion is expected to dominate and measured the mean square displacement (MSD) of the plasmid. Unlike at the longer timescale, we found a linear dependence on time, and a diffusion coefficient of (2.01±0.14) x 10–4 μm2s–1 consistent with, and in support of, the over-damped spring model (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G.

claim: Neither the DNA relay model nor the Brownian Ratchet model exhibits true regular positioning.
source: There have been two stochastic molecular-level models of plasmid positioning to date. Though different in some details, both models propose that elastic fluctuations of DNA and/or protein bonds power movement of plasmids up a gradient of DNA bound ParA-ATP. However, neither model exhibits true regular positioning as we observed for F plasmid.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to existing models.

claim: In the DNA relay model, plasmids oscillate across the nucleoid with regular positioning emerging only as a time-averaging effect.
source: In the DNA relay model (Surovtsev et al., 2016a), plasmids oscillate across the nucleoid, reversing direction upon reaching either a pole or another plasmid, with regular positioning emerging from these oscillations only as a time-averaging effect.
evidence: This is a description of the DNA relay model from Surovtsev et al., 2016a.

claim: In the Brownian Ratchet model, plasmids exhibit 'local excursions' around home positions determined by segregation distance upon replication.
source: In the Brownian Ratchet model (Hu et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017) on the other hand, plasmids exhibit 'local excursions' around home positions that are determined by the distance they segregate upon replication.
evidence: This is a description of the Brownian Ratchet model from Hu et al., 2017.

claim: Regular positioning can be achieved through balancing of diffusive fluxes of nucleoid-bound ParA-ATP into the plasmid from each longitudinal direction.
source: Ietswaart et al. have previously shown that regular positioning can theoretically be achieved, independently of the particular mechanism of force generation, through the balancing of the diffusive fluxes of nucleoid-bound ParA-ATP into the plasmid from each longitudinal direction.
evidence: This is based on work by Ietswaart et al.

claim: A critical component of the flux balance mechanism is that ParA-ATP dimers must diffuse on the nucleoid sufficiently far before hydrolysing ATP and unbinding.
source: It was also realised that a critical component of the mechanism is that the ParA-ATP dimers must diffuse on the nucleoid sufficiently far before hydrolysing ATP and unbinding (Murray and Howard, 2019; Subramanian and Murray, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murray and Howard, 2019 and Subramanian and Murray, 2021.

claim: The threshold diffusive length-scale for regular positioning decreases with the number of plasmids.
source: Note that the threshold decreases with the number of plasmids - with each additional plasmid, a shorter distance needs to be 'sensed' per plasmid.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the flux balance mechanism.

claim: Sensing between plasmids occurs through competition for the same ParA-ATP dimers.
source: Sensing between plasmids occurs through competition for the same ParA-ATP dimers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Diffusion of ParA-ATP dimers on the nucleoid has been observed in vitro using single-particle microscopy.
source: The diffusion of ParA dimers on the nucleoid referred to above could occur through hopping of dimers between DNA strands during transient unbinding events or through the direct contact of DNA strands. Indeed, this has been argued to be essential for ParA gradient formation in Caulobacter crescentus (Surovtsev et al., 2016b) and was observed in vitro using single-particle microscopy (Vecchiarelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Surovtsev et al., 2016b and Vecchiarelli et al., 2013.

claim: The transition from static to diffusive to oscillatory can be understood in terms of differing timescales of tether dissociation and ParA repletion rate.
source: This transition from static to diffusive to oscillatory can be understood in the terms of the differing timescale of tether dissociation on the one hand and the ParA repletion rate on the other (Hu et al., 2015; Walter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results based on previous work.

claim: In the oscillatory regime, tethers break faster than they can be replaced, leading to a ParA depletion zone behind the plasmid.
source: In the oscillatory regime, tethers break (due to ATP hydrolysis) faster than they can be replaced. This leads to a ParA depletion zone behind the plasmid that reinforces its movement in the same direction.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying oscillatory dynamics.

claim: F plasmid dynamics sit within the regular positioning regime but not far from the interfacial region of confined oscillations.
source: Interestingly, these parameter values suggest that while the dynamics of a single F plasmid sits within the regular positioning regime, it is not far from the interfacial region of confined oscillations.
evidence: This is inferred from the position of F plasmid in the phase diagram.

claim: Only the parameters D_h and k_h (which determine λ and ε) can push the system into static or oscillatory regimes.
source: Finally, we explored how the other parameters of the model affect the dynamics. We varied the main parameters across four orders of magnitude centred on the set used in Figure 4 (which lies in the regular positioning regime). We found that only the two parameters varied in our sweep were able to push the system into the static or oscillatory regimes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The model can reproduce quarter positioning for two plasmids irrespective of initial positions.
source: We next considered the case of cells having two and more plasmids. We found that our model could reproduce the same quarter positioning as observed for F plasmid (Figure 5A). Importantly, regular positioning was achieved irrespective of where the two plasmids were initially positioned.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Simulated replicated plasmids move apart rapidly towards quarter positions similar to experimental observations.
source: We also simulated plasmid replication by duplicating one plasmid during the simulation. We found that the replicated plasmids moved apart rapidly towards the quarter positions in a qualitatively similar way as we observed in our experimental data (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Multiple F plasmid cell cycles show initial stable mid-cell positioning transitioning to low-amplitude oscillations as cell length increases.
source: Motivated by these results, we went back to our F plasmid data and examined cells harbouring one plasmid with greater than average cell length. Consistent with our simulations, we found multiple cell cycles in which the plasmid was initially stably positioned at mid-cell but as the length of the cell increased, appeared to display low-amplitude oscillations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For F plasmid with one plasmid, there is a marked increase in the proportion of oscillatory segments from cell lengths of about 3 μm, with up to 50% of timepoints classified as oscillatory.
source: Binning the individual time-points from these classified segments according to cell length revealed the relative abundance of the two populations (Figure 6C). We found a marked increase in the proportion of oscillatory segments from cell lengths of about 3 μm, with up to 50% of timepoints being classified as oscillatory, consistent with our prediction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cells with two F plasmids show a significantly smaller proportion of oscillatory segments and weaker length dependence than cells with one plasmid.
source: Interestingly, the same analysis on cells containing two plasmids revealed a significantly smaller proportion of oscillatory segments and a weaker length dependence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ParA-ATP dimers diffuse a distance of about 1.5 μm before dissociating.
source: More specifically, these results suggest that ParA-ATP dimers diffuse a distance of about 1.5 μm before dissociating.
evidence: This is inferred from the threshold length-scale data in Figure 6D.

claim: Oscillatory behaviour of F plasmid decreases upon plasmid replication within individual cells.
source: We also examined how oscillations are affected by changes in plasmid number within individual cells i.e. upon plasmid replication (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). We found that oscillatory behaviour appeared to decrease in that a classification of oscillatory dynamics before replication was not a reliable indicator of oscillatory dynamics afterwards.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a rapid decay in the autocorrelation for F plasmid containing an oscillatory trajectory segment across generations.
source: The same was true across generations - we observed a rapid decay in the autocorrelation for containing an oscillatory trajectory segment (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: pB171 has a copy number comparable to F plasmid.
source: Using a previously constructed TetR/tetO labelling system, we first determined the copy number of this system and found it to be comparable to F plasmid (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: pB171 exhibits clear unambiguous oscillatory behaviour in ~80% of cells containing a single plasmid.
source: We then examined plasmid dynamics in cells containing a single plasmid and found clear unambiguous oscillatory behaviour in ~80% of such cells (Figure 7A), in stark contrast to F plasmid (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The position distribution of pB171 is flat-topped, different from F plasmid and similar to the oscillatory regime of the model.
source: This was reflected in the flat-topped plasmid position distribution (Figure 7B), which was very different from that of F plasmid and more similar to what we obtained in the oscillatory regime of our model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The position and velocity autocorrelations of pB171 show oscillatory dynamics including positive velocity autocorrelation between consecutive frames.
source: More importantly, the oscillatory nature of the dynamics was reflected in the position and velocity autocorrelations (Figure 7C and D), including a positive velocity autocorrelation between consecutive frames, which is a signature of processive motion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The autocorrelation curves of pB171 qualitatively match those obtained in the oscillatory regime of the model.
source: These curves qualitatively matched those obtained in our model within the oscillatory regime (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Oscillations in pB171 are almost four times as likely as in F plasmid overall.
source: Overall oscillations were almost four times as likely for pB171 as for F plasmid (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Oscillations in pB171 are much less apparent in cells with two plasmids.
source: However, this was much reduced when we considered cells with two plasmids, for which oscillations were much less apparent (Figure 7E and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both F plasmid and pB171 operate just below the threshold for oscillations, with pB171 crossing the threshold in cells with a single plasmid.
source: This suggests that, similar to F plasmid, the ParABS system of pB171 does not lie entirely within the oscillatory regime, but only enters it for cells containing a single plasmid, in which the sensing distance required for regular positioning is longest (see above).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and model predictions.

claim: The unified stochastic model explains all plasmid dynamics in terms of two dimensionless parameters λ and ε.
source: Together, these two parameters map out the entire space of plasmid dynamics and give a physical understanding of all possible dynamics including oscillations, regular positioning, static, diffusive, as well as whether the ParA distribution has a maximum or minimum at the cargo.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: ParABS regularly positions plasmids across the nucleoid but operates just below the threshold of an oscillatory instability.
source: Our results indicate that ParABS regularly positions plasmids across the nucleoid but operates just below the threshold of an oscillatory instability, which according to our model, minimises ATP consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Operating just below the oscillatory threshold minimises ATP consumption according to the model.
source: Our results indicate that ParABS regularly positions plasmids across the nucleoid but operates just below the threshold of an oscillatory instability, which according to our model, minimises ATP consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The oscillatory regime consumes the least ATP because it has the least flux of ParA-ATP dimers into the plasmid.
source: Interestingly, we found that the oscillatory regime consumed the least ATP (Figure 8B). This is because this regime has the least flux of ParA-ATP dimers into the plasmid due to the short distance ParA dimers diffuse before dissociating from the DNA despite the fact that the plasmid moves back and forth across the nucleoid i.e. the directed movement of the plasmids cannot compensate for the reduced incoming flux of ParA dimers.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and explained in the text.

claim: The oscillatory regime has the fewest simultaneous ParA-plasmid tethers.
source: Consistent with this, the oscillatory regime has the fewest simultaneous ParA-plasmid tethers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Brownian Ratchet model found single plasmids to exhibit 'local excursions' (approximate positioning) rather than regular positioning.
source: This explains why this study found single plasmids to exhibit 'local excursions' around mid-cell, that is approximate rather than regular positioning (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an explanation of why the Brownian Ratchet model did not show regular positioning.

claim: The model uses strain DLT3125 for F plasmid experiments, a derivative of E. coli K-12 strain DLT1215 containing mini-F plasmid derivative pJYB234.
source: F plasmid experiments use strain DLT3125 (Sanchez et al., 2015), a derivative of the E. coli K-12 strain DLT1215 (Bouet et al., 2005) containing the mini-F plasmid derivative pJYB234.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: pB171 experiments use strain SR1, a derivative of E. coli K-12 containing a ΔpcnB mutation.
source: Experiments on plasmid pB171, use strain SR1 (Ringgaard et al., 2009), a derivative of the E. coli K-12 strain containing a ΔpcnB mutation which reduces the copy number of the hosted pB171-derived plasmids.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The mean cell cycle duration for F plasmid experiments is 101.17±34.55 min.
source: The mean cell cycle duration is 101.17±34.55 min (mean ± s.d.).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mean cell length at birth for F plasmid experiments is 2.46±0.38 μm.
source: The mean length is 2.46±0.38 μm (mean ± s.d.) and 4.92±0.63 μm (mean ± s.d.) respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean cell length at division for F plasmid experiments is 4.92±0.63 μm.
source: The mean length is 2.46±0.38 μm (mean ± s.d.) and 4.92±0.63 μm (mean ± s.d.) respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells have 1.9±0.78 ParB foci at birth and 3.58±0.96 foci at division.
source: Cells have 1.9±0.78 ParB foci (mean ± s.d.) at birth and 3.58±0.96 ParB foci (mean ± s.d.) at division.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
